slides.title: Catching the few bad transactions
points: A fraud model scores each transaction's risk so the riskiest can be blocked or reviewed.
Fraud is rare, fast-changing and adversarial: people actively try to get past the model.

slides.title: Features, labels, decisions
points: Features: amount, merchant, device, location, how this compares with the customer's usual behaviour, velocity (how many in the last hour).
Labels arrive late (chargebacks take weeks), so training data lags reality.
Rare positives: use PR AUC, class weights or resampling, and judge precision and recall at the operating threshold.
Scores become actions: approve, step-up check, manual review, block.

slides.title: Losses against friction
points: Blocking more stops more fraud and annoys more honest customers.
Fraudsters adapt, so performance decays; retrain often and monitor.
Rules and models together: rules for known patterns, the model for the rest.

slides.title: What it looks like
points: Real-time scoring under tight latency (tens of milliseconds).
A review queue sized to the team's capacity.
Feedback from reviewers fed back as labels.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Putting the best result first
points: Search ranking orders the results a search engine retrieves, so the most useful appear at the top.
It's usually a model trained on what people clicked, bought or applied to.

slides.title: Retrieve, then rank
points: Retrieval finds candidates fast (keyword and vector search); ranking scores a few hundred carefully.
Features: text match, freshness, popularity, personal signals, quality.
Learning-to-rank models (gradient-boosted trees, neural rankers) optimise the order, measured by NDCG or precision at k.
Clicks are biased by position: people click the top more because it's at the top.

slides.title: Relevance, freshness, fairness
points: Optimising clicks can reward clickbait; use stronger signals (purchases, long dwell).
Personalisation helps relevance and narrows what people see.
Offline gains need online A/B tests to confirm.

slides.title: What it looks like
points: Logged impressions with positions, so position bias can be corrected.
Human-rated query sets for offline evaluation.
Business rules after ranking (no unavailable items).

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Answering customers from your own help content
points: A support assistant answers questions using the help centre, policies and the customer's own account, and hands off to people when it should.
It's a RAG system with permissions, tone and escalation.

slides.title: Ground, cite, escalate
points: Retrieve from approved help articles, filtered by product and region.
Account data (orders, plan) comes through tools that only see that customer's records.
Answers cite their sources; with no good source, say so and offer a person.
Escalate on frustration, money, legal or safety topics, or low confidence.

slides.title: Deflection against trust
points: Answering more questions automatically saves cost and risks confident wrong answers.
Stale help articles produce stale answers; content needs owners.
Customers need to know they're talking to AI and how to reach a person.

slides.title: What it looks like
points: An eval set built from real tickets, with correct answers.
Resolution rate and escalation rate tracked together, not deflection alone.
Human review of a sample of conversations each week.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: A model that completes a task in steps
points: An agent uses tools (search, a calendar, a database) in a loop to finish a multi-step task, such as 'find three suitable flights and draft an email'.
Its value and its risk both come from acting, not just answering.

slides.title: Plan, act, check
points: Give a clear goal, a few well-described tools, and limits (steps, budget, time).
The loop: choose a tool, run it, read the result, decide the next step.
Check progress against the goal; stop when done or stuck.
Irreversible actions wait for a person's confirmation.

slides.title: Autonomy against reliability
points: Each step can fail; a ten-step task with 95 % per-step success fails often.
Long runs cost more and are harder to debug.
Narrower agents (one job, few tools) are far more reliable than general ones.

slides.title: What it looks like
points: Every step traced, so failures can be replayed.
Evals on whole tasks, measuring success rate, cost and steps.
Fallback to a person when the agent stops making progress.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Design an ML-powered product feature
points: You're asked to design something like a feed ranker, a spam filter or a recommendation system end to end.
They score how you frame the problem, the data, the model, evaluation and serving — not just the algorithm.

slides.title: A structure to follow
points: Clarify the goal and how success is measured, online and offline.
Data: sources, labels, how fresh, how biased.
Model: a simple baseline first, then what you'd add; features and how they're computed.
Serving and monitoring: latency, scale, drift, feedback loops.

slides.title: Practical over fancy
points: Jumping to a deep model before discussing data and metrics loses points.
Say what you'd ship first and how you'd learn from it.
Name risks: leakage, cold start, bias, feedback loops.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Practise four or five classic ML designs out loud.
Always define the metric before the model.
Draw the data flow from raw events to predictions and back.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Something is wrong with a model; find it
points: You're told a model behaves badly (great offline, poor online; suddenly worse; unfair to a group) and asked how you'd investigate.
They're checking for a methodical approach.

slides.title: Data first
points: Check the data pipeline: did inputs change, break or go missing?
Compare training and production feature distributions (skew, drift).
Look for leakage that inflated offline results.
Slice errors by segment to find where it fails.

slides.title: Hypotheses, not guesses
points: Retraining immediately can hide the cause and repeat it.
Most model problems are data problems.
Say what evidence would confirm or rule out each hypothesis.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Practise a checklist: data, features, labels, split, metric, serving.
Prepare a story of a real model you debugged.
Talk through the cheapest checks first.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

newQuestions.stem: Your fraud model is trained on last year's chargebacks. Labels for the last six weeks aren't in yet. What's the risk?
choices: The newest fraud patterns aren't in training; monitor recent performance and use faster signals (reviewer decisions, customer reports) as interim labels
The model will overfit to six weeks
why: Fraud changes quickly; delayed labels mean the model learns old tactics.
Recency matters more than volume here.
It's missing them, not overfitting to them.
They're the most reliable label, just slow.

newQuestions.stem: A ranking model trained on clicks keeps promoting whatever is already at the top. Why?
choices: Position bias: top results get more clicks because of their position; correct for it (randomised slots, inverse propensity weighting)
why: Without correcting for position, the model learns 'being on top earns clicks'.
Size doesn't remove the bias.
They aren't random; they're biased.
Not the cause.

newQuestions.stem: A customer asks the support assistant to reverse a large charge. Policy for refunds over a threshold isn't in the help centre. What should the assistant do?
choices: Say it can't decide that, and hand the customer to a person with the context so far
Approve the refund to keep the customer happy
Invent a policy that sounds reasonable
why: Money decisions without a source belong with a person, and the hand-off saves the customer repeating themselves.
It has no authority or policy for that.
That's a hallucinated commitment.
Unhelpful and frustrating.

newQuestions.stem: An agent succeeds at each step 95 % of the time and needs 12 steps per task. Roughly how often does a whole task succeed, and what helps?
choices: About 54 % (0.95¹²); fewer, more reliable steps and checks between them help
why: Errors compound; shortening the chain and verifying steps raises task success.
Each step is another chance to fail.
Failures multiply, they don't average out.
They often do, at that rate about half the time.

newQuestions.stem: In an ML system design round for a spam filter, what should come before choosing a model?
choices: The goal and metrics (which mistakes cost more), the data and labels, and how predictions will be used
why: Framing decides everything else and is a big part of the score.
Model choice without framing looks naive.
Hardware comes far later.
Implementation detail too early.

newQuestions.stem: A model's online accuracy dropped sharply yesterday. What do you check first?
choices: The input data: a broken upstream pipeline, missing or changed features, a new data source
why: A sudden drop with no model change usually means the inputs changed.
It didn't change yesterday.
Training detail, not a sudden online change.
Doesn't address a sudden drop.
